To fix (3)

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 5 imprecise p values out of 60 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
ps ≥ .076 The anhedonia × condition, anhedonia × time window, and three-way interactions were not statistically significant (all ps ≥ .076; see Supplementary
ps ≥ .057 For positive and neutral stimuli, anhedonia did not show significant associations with pleasantness, unpleasantness or arousal ratings (all ps ≥ .057).
ps ≥ .072 None of the individual anhedonia slopes within each condition and time window differed significantly from zero (all ps ≥ .072; see Supplementary Tables S6a-b).
ps ≥ .494 Neither the anhedonia × condition nor the three-way interaction was statistically significant (both ps ≥ .494; see Supplementary Tables S9a-b).
ps ≥ .076 None of these associations were significantly moderated by valence (all ps ≥ .076; see Supplementary Tables S13-S16).

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

README Files

README files are a way to document the contents and structure of a folder, helping users locate the information they need. You can use a README to document changes to a repository, and explain how files are named. Please consider adding a README to each repository or including ‘README’ in the name of your overview document.

Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 18 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (18). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a ._ copy of a .csv for data).

Remove these: Operating system files: macOS adds a __MACOSX folder and a ._ copy of every file it puts in a zip, and .DS_Store files to folders; Windows adds Thumbs.db and desktop.ini. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with zip -r -X, or remove them afterwards with zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store". RStudio session files (.Rproj.user/) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; R history (.Rhistory, .Rapp.history) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; Jupyter checkpoints (.ipynb_checkpoints/) are automatic copies of notebooks; compiled Python files (__pycache__/, .pyc) are recreated when the code runs; open-document lock files (~$...docx, .~lock...#) are left while a document is open; editor backups (file~, .bak, .swp) and temporary files (.tmp, .temp, an interrupted save of R’s workspace, .RDataTmp) are copies a program made by itself.

Keep only on purpose: version control folders (.git, .svn, .hg) hold the project’s history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; editor settings (.idea, .vscode) can hold paths on your own computer. A .gitignore based on GitHub’s templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 23 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.

Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167.

For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see Improving Your Statistical Inferences.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. setwd() calls were found in 7 code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). install.packages() calls were found in 7 code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 1 code file, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 16 distinct packages/libraries: car, dplyr, effectsize, emmeans, ggplot2, gtools, lme4, lmerTest, parameters, renv, report, rstatix, sjPlot, stringr, tidyr, tidyverse. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

Reproducible Environment

No renv.lock file, sessionInfo()/session_info() record, or groundhog/checkpoint date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an renv.lock (via the renv package), a sessionInfo() text dump, or a groundhog/checkpoint date-pin alongside the code.

What we found

  • We classified 96 files: 29 data, 7 code, 1 documentation, 55 materials, 4 unknown.
  • We found 29 tabular data files and extracted 487 columns from 28 of them.
  • We grouped the files into 1 study group (ex1).
  • 1 file read as a table but is not a usable rectangular dataset (btf_scr_pic_v01.txt: 100% of columns are free text, not variables). No columns were extracted and they were not sent to the LLM. Share the underlying data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable) with a codebook: btf_scr_pic_v01.txt. We ran automated data-quality checks on 487 columns; 2 columns have at least one potential issue (2 columns with leading/trailing whitespace).

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 487 columns across 28 data files.

Issues Identified

2 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

File Column Issues
long.behav.pic.pro.csv ID ↔︎️ Whitespace — 1 value with leading/trailing whitespace: ” BTF_001_PIC_PRO”
long.behav.pic.pro.viv.csv ID ↔︎️ Whitespace — 1 value with leading/trailing whitespace: ” BTF_001_PIC_PRO”

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 28 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

  • 16 installable dependencies detected.
  • 1120 statistics stored from the extracted output; 1 of 57 reported tests matched (1.8%).

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

A script starts a program outside R or Python.

  • Analysis Behavioral Data.R starts xdg-open.

The computer we run the code on does not have this program, so we could not check these scripts; this need not be a fault of the code. Name the program, its version and where to get it in the README. A Docker image can include it.

R or Python could not read a script, because of a mistake in the code itself.

  • BTF_LPP_ENCODING_ANALYSIS.R
  • BTF_LPP_PROSPECTION_ANALYSIS.R
  • BTF_LPP_RECALL_ANALYSIS.R
  • LPP Analyses PIC BASE Stimulus offset.R
  • LPP Analyses PIC BASE.R

Run each script once in a fresh session before you deposit it; the error message shows the line to fix.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 7 scripts: 1 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 5 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

setwd() in the code

7 scripts call setwd(). This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after ignoring a setwd() that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed.

Reproducible after removing setwd(): BTF_SCR_Analyses.R.

Calls that install packages in the code

58 calls to install.packages(), groundhog, checkpoint, renv, pacman and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: groundhog.library() and p_load() by library(), the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.
