Discussion

The present study examined how anhedonia relates to late positive potential (LPP) amplitudes, subjective emotional responses, and mental imagery vividness during the encoding, recall, and prospection of emotionally salient events in a healthy community sample. The central finding was that, whereas higher anhedonia was associated with larger LPP amplitudes during encoding without significant differences across valence conditions, it was associated with reduced positive-neutral LPP differentiation during subsequent recall.

Specifically, higher anhedonia was associated with relatively lower LPP amplitudes during positive compared with neutral recall between 1,000 and 3,000 ms and compared with negative recall between 2,000 and 3,000 ms. In contrast, no significant differences in anhedonia slopes emerged between negative and neutral recall across any time window.

This pattern was accompanied by a smaller positive-neutral difference in subjective pleasantness ratings. Together, these findings provide preliminary evidence that anhedonia may be characterized less by diminished pleasure in response to immediate positive stimulation than by difficulties reinstating positive affect when rewarding experiences are mentally recalled. Such difficulties may represent a mechanism linking anhedonia to motivational impairment, as diminished affective responses to recalled positive experiences may weaken the internal representation of reward value needed to sustain reward anticipation and goal-directed behavior (Pillny, Edwards, & Riehle, 2026; Strauss & Gold, 2012; Zou et al., 2026).

The attenuated LPP differentiation during positive recall may reflect reduced sustained attentional engagement with, or elaborative processing of, positive memory content. This interpretation is consistent with evidence linking the LPP to sustained attention and elaborative processing of motivationally salient information (Hajcak et al., 2010; Weinberg & Hajcak, 2010) and linking anhedonia to difficulties in representing the subjective value of impending rewards across mental health conditions (Gold et al., 2012; Waltz & Gold, 2016; Xia et al., 2026).

Simultaneous EEG-fMRI research has shown that LPP amplitudes during pleasant picture viewing covary with activity in regions implicated in reward processing and appetitive motivation, including the medial prefrontal cortex and nucleus accumbens (Liu et al., 2012).

Notably, these regions are also selectively recruited during pleasant mental imagery (Costa et al., 2010), suggesting partially overlapping neural substrates for processing positive external stimuli and internally generated positive experiences. Although the LPP is not a specific measure of reward processing, these converging findings support the possibility that reduced LPP differentiation during positive recall reflects diminished engagement with the motivational significance of positive mental representations. In turn, such diminished engagement may contribute to difficulties in generating anticipatory pleasure and translating remembered positive experiences into future goal-directed behavior (Pillny et al., 2024; Weittenhiller et al., 2020).

Nevertheless, the direction and developmental trajectory of the relationship between anhedonia, attenuated LPP responses during positive recall, and impoverished mental representations remains unclear. Specifically, it is uncertain whether alterations in the neural processing of positive mental representations contribute to anhedonia, arise as a consequence of it, or reflect reciprocal influences. On the one hand, previous LPP research suggests that anhedonia may, at least in part, be associated with diminished recruitment of neural processes involved in the affective and motivational evaluation of positive stimuli (Dell'Acqua et al., 2026; Santopetro et al., 2026). On the other hand, a growing body of behavioral evidence links anhedonia to impairments in the generation and quality of mental representations (Barry et al., 2021; Hallford et al., 2018; Pillny, Edwards, MacLeod, et al., 2026; Pillny et al., 2024; Pillny et al., 2022). Consistent with this evidence, higher anhedonia in the present study was associated with lower mental imagery vividness across all three valence conditions, suggesting a relatively valence-independent reduction in representational quality. Such impoverished representations may, in turn, elicit weaker affective responses at both the neural and subjective levels, which is potentially similarly reflected in attenuated LPP amplitudes observed during positive recall. Conversely, reduced LPP amplitudes may reflect diminished motivated attention or affective elaboration of otherwise intact mental representations, rather than deficits in their generation or quality. Yet these explanations are not mutually exclusive. Impoverished representations may limit emotional engagement, while reduced motivational and attentional engagement may further constrain the elaboration and maintenance of emotionally salient representations.

Importantly, the absence of a valence-specific association between anhedonia and LPP amplitudes during prospection, despite reduced imagery vividness across valences, suggests that diminished representational quality alone may not be sufficient to explain the observed neural alterations. Instead, the relationship between anhedonia and neural responses to mental representations may depend on the specific cognitive operations involved in processing versus recalling or constructing emotional experiences.

The non-significant association between anhedonia and subjective pleasantness ratings during prospection was unexpected. Episodic future thinking impairments have been associated with psychopathology and particularly anhedonia (Hallford et al., 2018; Pillny, Edwards, MacLeod, et al., 2026; Raffard et al., 2013; Teague et al., 2026). One possible explanation for the present findings concerns the fixed task sequence employed in the current study, in which prospection always followed recall and both tasks drew on the same previously encoded stimuli. In populations without mental health diagnoses, episodic future simulations rely, at least in part, on the retrieval and recombination of episodic information whereas people with schizophrenia have been found to show a reduced association between memory retrieval and episodic future thinking when relative to controls (Barry et al., 2020; Painter & Kring, 2015). Furthermore, previous research has shown that guided recall of positive memories can enhance anticipatory pleasure and motivation in individuals with schizophrenia (Edwards et al., 2020; Painter & Kring, 2016). Accordingly, the preceding recall task may have enhanced the generation of subsequent future simulations, potentially attenuating individual differences in neural responses associated with anhedonia.

Importantly, despite the absence of significant LPP associations, the relationships between anhedonia and subjective emotional responses during prospection broadly resembled those observed during recall, albeit somewhat less pronounced. Thus, the null LPP findings should not be interpreted as evidence that emotional processing during future simulation is unaffected by anhedonia. Future studies employing counterbalanced task orders or prospection tasks without preceding recall are needed to determine whether the observed dissociation between neural and subjective responses reflects task-related facilitation or genuine differences in the emotional processing of remembered versus imagined future experiences.

During stimulus encoding, we found no evidence that associations between anhedonia and LPP amplitudes differed significantly across valence conditions. Although higher anhedonia was associated with larger LPP amplitudes overall, subjective pleasantness and arousal responses to positive stimuli were not significantly associated with anhedonia.

These findings are consistent with meta-analytic evidence suggesting relatively preserved LPP responses to positive stimuli in schizophrenia and intact within-person LPP differentiation in depressive disorders (Castro et al., 2019; Dell'Acqua et al., 2026), as well as relatively preserved subjective positive affect and arousal responses in schizophrenia (Llerena et al., 2012; Riehle et al., 2024). At the same time, other meta-analyses have reported attenuated subjective positive affect in depressive disorders (Bylsma et al., 2008) and a small but significant association between attenuated LPP responses and greater depressive symptom severity (Santopetro et al., 2026). Although these inconsistencies may partly reflect disorder-specific patterns of affective and reward dysfunction (Pillny, Renz, et al., 2026; Zou et al., 2026), much of the existing evidence derives from diagnostic group comparisons, making it difficult to isolate associations specifically attributable to anhedonia from those related to other clinical characteristics. By examining anhedonia dimensionally in a nonclinical sample, the present study offers a complementary perspective that may be less susceptible to confounding by factors such as medication use and depressed mood.

Nevertheless, the absence of significant associations should not be interpreted as definitive evidence of preserved hedonic functioning, particularly given the restricted range of anhedonia in our sample and the possibility of different patterns in clinical populations.

Subject to replication in samples spanning a broader range of anhedonia severity, our findings are consistent with relatively preserved immediate affective responses to positive stimuli. This possibility challenges a strictly hedonic conceptualization of anhedonia as a generalized inability to experience pleasure and suggests that difficulties in generating positive affect may depend on whether rewarding experiences are directly encountered or mentally represented.

Importantly, the present findings suggest that alterations in affective responding associated with anhedonia extend beyond diminished positive affect. Higher anhedonia was associated not only with reduced pleasantness during positive recall but, across tasks, also with greater unpleasantness in response to positive and neutral content, alongside greater pleasantness and reduced unpleasantness in response to negative content. This broader pattern is consistent with recent accounts of anhedonia that emphasize alterations in both positive and negative affective processing (Edwards et al., 2026; Pillny, Edwards, & Riehle, 2026). Specifically, heightened unpleasantness toward neutral stimuli and positive mental representations is compatible with a diminished positivity offset, whereby positive affect is less likely to outweigh negative affect under conditions of weak or ambiguous emotional stimulation (Bartolomeo et al., 2023; Gollan et al., 2016; Riehle et al., 2022; Strauss et al., 2017). Additional mechanisms, including reward devaluation, fear of happiness (Gallagher et al., 2024), and avoidance of positive stimuli (Winer & Salem, 2016) could help to explain why positive mental representations evoke greater unpleasantness in individuals with higher anhedonia. Furthermore, the combination of reduced pleasantness toward positive representations and attenuated unpleasantness toward negative content is compatible with emotion context insensitivity, characterized by diminished affective differentiation across emotional valences (Rottenberg & Hindash, 2015). Although these mechanisms were not directly assessed, they offer complementary explanations for the observed alterations in emotional responding.

Limitations

Participants were recruited from a nonclinical community sample. Although this approach allowed us to examine dimensional associations between anhedonia and affective responding while minimizing potential confounding by clinical features such as depressed mood, hopelessness, delusions, or hallucinations, it also restricted the observed range of anhedonia severity. In particular, SHAPS scores remained below empirically established thresholds for clinically significant anhedonia (Ho et al., 2024). Consequently, the findings cannot be readily generalized to individuals experiencing clinically relevant anhedonia or psychiatric disorders. Moreover, recalling and imagining emotional events require cognitive effort, and the willingness to invest such effort may vary as a function of anhedonia. Given previous evidence linking anhedonia to reduced effort expenditure (Pillny, Renz, et al., 2026), we cannot rule out the possibility that the observed associations partly reflect reduced task engagement rather than alterations in the processing of mental representations per se.

However, additional exploratory analyses examining associations between anhedonia and self-reported effort, as well as between effort and imagery vividness, provided no indication that differences in subjective effort ratings accounted for the present findings.

Conclusion

Taken together, the present findings provide preliminary evidence that anhedonia is associated with attenuated LPP responses and diminished subjective pleasantness during positive relative to neutral recall, suggesting that altered affective processing of mental representations may contribute to difficulties in reward anticipation and motivated behavior.

Moreover, the findings indicate anhedonia to be associated with heightened unpleasantness in response to positive and neutral content alongside attenuated negative affective responses to negative content. This broader pattern suggests reduced affective differentiation across emotional valences, broadly consistent with accounts of emotion context insensitivity. Notably, the association between anhedonia and diminished neural differentiation of positive from neutral content emerged during recall but not during direct stimulus exposure, highlighting the potential importance of cognitive processes involved in retrieving emotional experiences. Whether these alterations reflect impoverished mental representations, diminished affective engagement with otherwise intact representations, or reciprocal influences remains subject to future research.
